If you want to bypass this version check, you can set the "pmOnFail" configuration to "warn" or "ignore" (e.g. via --pm-on-fail=ignore). If using "devEngines.packageManager", you can set its "onFail" to "warn" or "ignore"

aube doctor will print the version from devEngines though:
version:
  aube           1.37.0
  build-profile  release
  target         macos
  arch           aarch64"},{"number":1240,"title":"minimumReleaseAge does not reject young lockfile pins the way pnpm 11 does","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1240","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T06:23:11Z","bodyText":"Repo / case: https://github.com/mwolson/tmp-aube-issues/tree/main/pnpm-min-release-age
aube: 1.37.0
native pnpm: 11.20.0
Category: Troubleshooting and Bugs

Summary
aube documents minimumReleaseAge: 1440 by default (matching pnpm 11), but under default settings it still installs package versions that native pnpm 11 rejects for being too young. The practical gaps are:

Lockfile re-verification: pnpm fails installs when a committed lockfile pins a version younger than minimumReleaseAge (ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION). aube installs that lockfile successfully.
Cold resolve of a young exact pin: with only a just-published exact version available, pnpm fails (ERR_PNPM_NO_MATURE_MATCHING_VERSION). aube installs it because minimumReleaseAgeStrict defaults to false and falls back to the young pin.

Setting minimumReleaseAgeStrict: true makes aube reject on resolve (ERR_AUBE_NO_MATURE_MATCHING_VERSION). That is a useful control, but it is not pnpm 11’s default, and it still does not cover lockfile supply-chain re-verification.
Real-world trigger
In a monorepo with packageManager: pnpm@11.10.0 and no explicit minimumReleaseAge key (so pnpm 11’s 1440 default applies), a same-day pin of @opencode-ai/sdk@0.0.0-beta-202608061351 caused native pnpm to fail with:
[ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION] 1 lockfile entries failed verification:
  @opencode-ai/sdk@0.0.0-beta-202608061351 was published at 2026-08-06T14:17:07.289Z,
  within the minimumReleaseAge cutoff (...)

The same tree installed successfully under aube (via aubeshim’s pnpm shim) with no age rejection.
That specific beta will age past 24h; the minimal repro below does not depend on it.
Minimal repro
git clone https://github.com/mwolson/tmp-aube-issues.git
cd tmp-aube-issues/pnpm-min-release-age
# needs: aube, real pnpm 11 (not an aubeshim shim), node, curl
# optional: PNPM_BIN=/path/to/real/pnpm
./repro.sh; echo exit=$?
Exit 1 while the gap is present. The script starts a local mock registry that always reports publishedAt=now for a tiny fresh-pkg@1.0.0, then compares:

Scenario A: seed a lockfile with minimumReleaseAge: 0, flip to 1440, reinstall

pnpm → ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION
aube → installs


Scenario B: cold resolve under minimumReleaseAge: 1440

pnpm → ERR_PNPM_NO_MATURE_MATCHING_VERSION
aube → installs


Scenario C (control): aube with minimumReleaseAgeStrict: true → ERR_AUBE_NO_MATURE_MATCHING_VERSION

Docs checked

https://aube.jdx.dev/security (minimumReleaseAge default 1440; strict opt-in)
https://aube.jdx.dev/settings/#setting-minimumreleaseage
https://aube.jdx.dev/settings/#setting-minimumreleaseagestrict
https://pnpm.io/supply-chain-security
Related but different: #1191 (outdated/update listing age-gated packages)

Expected
For pnpm-compatible projects that rely on the default 24h age gate:

Installing from a lockfile that pins a too-young version should fail (or at least warn hard), matching pnpm’s lockfile supply-chain verification.
Optionally, default behavior for young exact pins should match pnpm more closely, or docs should call out that aube’s non-strict fallback and missing lockfile age re-check are intentional differences from pnpm 11.

Actual (aube 1.37.0)
Young pins install under the documented default minimumReleaseAge: 1440 with minimumReleaseAgeStrict: false, including from existing lockfiles.
Happy to adjust the repro or wording if maintainers prefer framing this as a docs/parity clarification rather than a bug."},{"number":1242,"title":"Hoisted monorepo: identical deps become separate realpaths per workspace package","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1242","updatedAt":"2026-08-10T14:47:04Z","bodyText":"Summary
In a small workspace monorepo, under node-linker=hoisted (or
AUBE_NODE_LINKER=hoisted), aube materializes the same resolved dependency
as separate real directories under each workspace package. Content can be
byte-identical (and individual files may even share inodes via hardlinks) while
the package-root realpath still differs. Node and bundlers then treat those as
multiple module instances.
Under aube isolated, importers share one physical instance via the virtual
store and symlinks.
Minimal public repro (aube 1.37.0, exits 1 when the hoisted realpaths differ):

https://github.com/mwolson/tmp-aube-issues/tree/main/hoisted-workspace-shared-dep-realpath

cd hoisted-workspace-shared-dep-realpath
./repro.sh
We hit this while using hoisted installs so Metro / Expo could see in-tree
package slots on a larger monorepo. Isolated is better for module identity;
hoisted is better for that tooling. Curious whether a middle ground is ever in
scope, or whether the intended guidance is simply isolated (or another package
manager) for this class of project. Totally fine if the answer is "out of
scope."
Observed on the repro (aube 1.37.0)
Two workspace packages (@repro/app, @repro/lib) both depend on
is-number@7.0.0.



Linker
packages/*/node_modules/is-number
Same realpath?




Isolated
Symlinks into node_modules/.aube/is-number@7.0.0/...
Yes


Hoisted
Real directories under each package (not symlinks)
No



On the hoisted install we also saw matching inodes for some files inside those
trees (store hardlinks), but the package root paths still differ, which is what
resolution uses.
package-import-method looks like it controls store import, not "one package
root path shared across workspace importers in hoisted mode." We may simply be
missing a setting.
Why it came up for us
On a larger Expo monorepo, hoisted install produced many physical copies of the
same pinned dependency under each workspace package (e.g. several
node_modules/effect trees). A Metro sourcemap listed multiple
node_modules/effect package roots in one app bundle. Some libraries care about
process-wide singleton modules (module path identity, not only version).
No need to dig into that app here; the tiny is-number workspace is enough to
show the layout difference.
Ideas that might help (not requests)
If this is something you would ever want to support, things that would have
helped include:

Under hoisted, when linking the same integrity/version into multiple
workspace node_modules/<pkg> slots, expose one package-root realpath
(symlink or equivalent) instead of distinct real directories, even if file
contents are already hardlinked.
A hybrid layout that stays in-tree for tools but keeps a single realpath per
resolution key.
Docs on the recommended Expo monorepo path if the answer is "prefer isolated
plus some Metro configuration."

If hoisted is intentionally npm-like separate package roots per workspace
package, that is useful to know so we can stop expecting path identity there.
Questions

Is multi-root layout under hoisted intentional for workspaces, or just how
the current linker landed?
Would shared package-root identity across workspace importers ever be in
scope for hoisted mode?
For Expo monorepos, is isolated plus Metro config the recommended path, and
is that documented?

No expectation of a feature from this; a short "won't do / use isolated" would
already help. Happy to adjust the repro if a different shape would be more
useful."},{"number":1250,"title":"Filtered production install with no GVS materializes the full lockfile on a cold store","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1250","updatedAt":"2026-08-09T22:15:15Z","bodyText":"I am trying to migrate from Bun, but face few issues. This is one of them, the following repro was generated by AI..
Summary
With Aube 1.38.0, a filtered production install using the isolated linker and --disable-global-virtual-store materializes package cells for the full compatible lockfile when the Aube store is cold.
The selected importers receive the correct links, but unrelated production and development packages are still physically written under the project-level node_modules/.aube. Repeating the identical install after aube clean, once the store is warm, materializes only the selected production packages.
This is particularly visible in a clean Docker build because copying the project-level node_modules into the runtime image also copies all of the unlinked package cells.
Environment
aube 1.38.0 linux-arm64 (2026-08-07)
node 24, Debian trixie-slim
node linker: isolated (default)
global virtual store: disabled for the install

Minimal reproduction
Create this workspace:
.
├── package.json
├── aube-workspace.yaml
└── packages
    ├── backend
    │   └── package.json
    ├── backend-two
    │   └── package.json
    └── frontend
        └── package.json

package.json:
{
  "name": "aube-filter-repro",
  "private": true,
  "packageManager": "aube@1.38.0"
}
aube-workspace.yaml:
packages:
  - packages/*
packages/backend/package.json:
{
  "name": "backend",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "is-number": "7.0.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "picocolors": "1.1.1"
  }
}
packages/backend-two/package.json:
{
  "name": "backend-two",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "yocto-queue": "1.2.2"
  }
}
packages/frontend/package.json:
{
  "name": "frontend",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "is-odd": "3.0.1"
  }
}
Generate the complete workspace lockfile without linking node_modules:
aube install --lockfile-only --recursive
On Linux, start with a cold Aube store and run:
aube clean

aube install \
  --frozen-lockfile \
  --production \
  --disable-global-virtual-store \
  --filter ./packages/backend \
  --filter ./packages/backend-two

find node_modules/.aube \
  -mindepth 1 \
  -maxdepth 1 \
  ! -name node_modules \
  -exec basename {} \; | sort
The cold install materializes:
is-number@6.0.0
is-number@7.0.0
is-odd@3.0.1
picocolors@1.1.1
yocto-queue@1.2.2

Only is-number@7.0.0 and yocto-queue@1.2.2 belong to the selected production graph. picocolors@1.1.1 is a dev dependency, while is-odd@3.0.1 and is-number@6.0.0 belong only to the unselected frontend importer.
Now clean and repeat the exact same install without clearing the Aube store:
aube clean

aube install \
  --frozen-lockfile \
  --production \
  --disable-global-virtual-store \
  --filter ./packages/backend \
  --filter ./packages/backend-two

find node_modules/.aube \
  -mindepth 1 \
  -maxdepth 1 \
  ! -name node_modules \
  -exec basename {} \; | sort
The warm install materializes the expected set:
is-number@7.0.0
yocto-queue@1.2.2

Expected behavior
The first cold install and subsequent warm installs should materialize the same filtered production package set. Packages reachable only through dev dependencies or unselected workspace importers should not be written to the project-level virtual store.
Observed impact
In a larger workspace, the cold install produced 1,411 package cells. Of those, 741 cells were outside the selected backend production graph and consumed approximately 574 MiB of apparent file size. The selected importers did not link those packages, but a Docker COPY of the complete project node_modules preserved all of the orphaned files in the runtime image.
Workaround
Prefetching the complete lockfile immediately before the filtered no-GVS install makes the materialization correct:
aube fetch --frozen-lockfile --recursive \
  && aube install \
    --frozen-lockfile \
    --production \
    --disable-global-virtual-store \
    --filter ./packages/backend \
    --filter ./packages/backend-two
With the workaround, the minimal reproduction contains only the two expected package cells. Enabling the global virtual store also avoids the project-level over-materialization, but it does not directly produce a self-contained node_modules tree suitable for copying into a runtime image."},{"number":1251,"title":"Auto-installed peer of a dev dependency is recorded and installed as a production dependency","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1251","updatedAt":"2026-08-09T22:14:33Z","bodyText":"I am trying to migrate from Bun, but face few issues. This is one of them, the following repro was generated by AI..
Summary
With autoInstallPeers: true, Aube records an auto-installed peer of a direct devDependency under the importer's dependencies section. As a result, aube install --production installs that peer even though the project has no production dependencies.
This appears related to discussion #1173 and PR #1178, which established that auto-installed peers can appear as importer dependencies. That fix filters them from aube outdated; it does not address their dependency classification or their inclusion in production installs.
Environment

Aube 1.38.0 (macos-arm64)
pnpm 11.21.0 used for comparison

Minimal reproduction
Create an empty directory containing only this package.json:
{
  "name": "aube-peer-production-repro",
  "private": true,
  "devDependencies": {
    "react-dom": "19.1.1"
  }
}
Generate the lockfile:
aube install --lockfile-only
Aube 1.38.0 writes the auto-installed React peer as an importer production dependency:
settings:
  autoInstallPeers: true

importers:
  .:
    dependencies:
      react:
        specifier: ^19.1.1
        version: 19.2.8
    devDependencies:
      react-dom:
        specifier: 19.1.1
        version: 19.1.1(react@19.2.8)
To demonstrate the production-install impact while avoiding any cold-store behavior, fetch the lock first and then install production dependencies without the global virtual store:
aube fetch --frozen-lockfile
aube install --frozen-lockfile --production --disable-global-virtual-store
aube list --prod
Actual result:
dependencies:
+ react@19.2.8

aube 1.38.0 by jdx.dev · ✓ installed 1 package

dependencies:
└── react 19.2.8

The exact auto-selected React version may change, but React is consistently placed in the production dependency set.
Expected result
The production dependency graph should be empty because the manifest contains no dependencies or optionalDependencies.
The peer should remain associated with the dev-only react-dom graph. For comparison, pnpm 11.21.0 with its default autoInstallPeers: true produces this importer:
importers:
  .:
    devDependencies:
      react-dom:
        specifier: 19.1.1
        version: 19.1.1(react@19.2.8)
Running pnpm install --prod then leaves no application packages in node_modules.
Workaround
Setting this in aube-workspace.yaml prevents undeclared peers from being promoted:
autoInstallPeers: false
Required peers must then be declared explicitly in the appropriate dependency section. An existing affected lockfile also needs to be regenerated or repaired; changing the setting alone does not reclassify entries already present in the importer.
Possible fix
When Aube auto-installs a peer for a direct dependency, preserve the dependency kind of the package that required it. In this reproduction, the peer context is needed only by a devDependency, so it should not become an importer production root."},{"number":1125,"title":"aube bugs","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1125","updatedAt":"2026-08-09T15:41:32Z","bodyText":"Once I updated to 1.33.1 I faced several bugs:

aubr doesn't complete for package.json scripts
aubr interactive run has flicker when scrolling/moving down and up the list
shims stopped working by some reason"},{"number":1234,"title":"Make `store prune` fail closed on incomplete index scans","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1234","updatedAt":"2026-08-06T19:16:54Z","bodyText":"store prune builds its keep-set from cached package indexes. In the current scan, errors while listing directories, reading entries or files, and parsing JSON are skipped. Pruning then continues with whatever hashes were collected successfully. Because files missing from that set become prune candidates, a skipped index is effectively treated as an index with no references.
I reproduced with a synthetic 14-byte file placed in Aube's store layout and a package index that referenced it. With a valid index, the file was kept:
reported files pruned: 0
fixture file after prune: present (14 bytes)

After replacing that index with malformed JSON, the same command exited successfully and deleted the file:
reported files pruned: 1
exit code: 0
fixture file after prune: missing

seems like store prune should require a complete, error-free index scan before deleting any store files. if so, both a real prune and --dry-run should return an error naming the affected path if an existing index directory cannot be listed or an index file cannot be read or parsed and no files should be deleted if there's a scan error.
I think malformed JSON should block pruning rather than implicitly invalidate that package index. Repairing or deliberately removing a bad index can be a separate action
This matters most on APFS and btrfs, where link counts do not reveal reflinked copies and the cached indexes are the remaining keep-set. Tests could cover malformed JSON, unreadable files and directories, dry-run using the same scan, and a failure encountered after valid indexes have already been scanned. Each case should exit nonzero and leave every store file in place.
PR #365 previously made pruning abort when its SQLite index could not be read. That implementation was later reverted, and PR #372 closed without merging. This asks for the same guard in the current JSON scanner, without bringing back SQLite.

Reviewing a dependency update usually means answering "what changed?" — which
means finding the package's repo or changelog. Today neither aube outdated
nor the update -i picker shows where a package lives, so that lookup is
manual (aube view <pkg> repository, or an aube bugs-style jump) once per
package, outside the flow where you're actually deciding what to update.
Wrapper tooling hits the same wall: outdated --json has
current/wanted/latest/dependencyType, so scripts that want to present
updates with links end up reading node_modules/<name>/package.json or making
per-package view calls.
Proposal
Surface a normalized repository/homepage URL where update decisions happen:

aube outdated --json — add a url field per package: the manifest
repository URL normalized to something clickable (strip git+/.git,
git:// → https://, expand user/repo shorthand), falling back to
homepage. Additive, so existing consumers are unaffected.
aube outdated table — a URL column, possibly only at wide terminal
widths or behind --long, to keep the default table tight.
aube update -i — show the URL on each picker row (or as the option
description), so "what changed?" is answerable mid-selection.

The data is already in the cached packuments aube fetched to compute
wanted/latest, so this adds no network requests.
Prior art

yarn outdated (classic) had a URL column and a color legend people still
miss.
bundle_update_interactive (Ruby) shows a changelog link per gem in its
picker and is the workflow this proposal is modeled on.
pnpm has neither, which is part of why wrapper scripts exist.

Scope notes

"Changelog URL" in the strict sense (finding CHANGELOG.md, a releases
page, or a diff link) requires probing and is out of scope here — the
normalized repo URL is the 90% case with zero extra requests. A later
releases-style helper could build on it.
Happy to implement this as a PR if the direction fits — wanted to settle
scope here first per the contributing guide."},{"number":1212,"title":"`aube deploy` doesn't preserve patches","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1212","updatedAt":"2026-08-02T16:59:00Z","bodyText":"Repro: https://github.com/hilja/aube-update-repro/tree/main/deploy

I was pulling my hair our earlier and realized I had to apply the patch manually in my docker, and then everything worked:
RUN git -C /app/node_modules/lighthouse apply /usr/src/app/patches/lighthouse@13.3.0.patch"},{"number":1197,"title":"Editing a declared patch file is neither rejected by frozen installs nor re-hashed by plain installs","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1197","updatedAt":"2026-08-01T20:33:33Z","bodyText":"aube: 1.36.0 linux-x64 (2026-07-29)
Repro: https://github.com/mwolson/tmp-aube-issues/tree/main/pnpm-patch-edit-stale-lock-hash (./repro.sh exits non-zero while the issue reproduces; needs a real pnpm via PNPM_BIN)

Setup
One dependency with a declared patch, lockfile created by native pnpm 10.24.0 so the recorded content hash is canonically pnpm's:
# pnpm-lock.yaml (excerpt)
patchedDependencies:
  '@isaacs/string-locale-compare@1.1.0':
    hash: c73fcd10c137b7e2a95f07c5e8b12d9cefceb2ed59b266ee19933c6b7c2f35bd
    path: patches/@isaacs__string-locale-compare@1.1.0.patch
Baseline aube install on this state is fine.
Steps
Change the patch file's content in place (the repro edits one added line's text), then:
CI=1 aube install --ignore-scripts            # succeeds silently
aube install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts  # succeeds silently
aube install --ignore-scripts                 # succeeds; see below
What happens


Both frozen forms accept the stale lockfile silently: the recorded hash is the sha256 of the previous patch content, the file on disk no longer matches, and nothing reports it.


The plain install applies the new patch content to the store (the installed file carries the edited line) but leaves the old hash in patchedDependencies, so the lockfile and the installation now permanently disagree. Every subsequent install keeps this split state; nothing ever repairs or reports it.


Native pnpm rejects the identical lockfile + patch state:
ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH  Cannot proceed with the frozen installation.
The current "patchedDependencies" configuration doesn't match the value found in the lockfile



The only tool-driven way I found to refresh the hash is aube install --force, which also re-resolves unrelated floating ranges (in the real workspace this pulled in newer expo/router versions as a side effect). The practical recovery was hand-editing the recorded hash, which the next install then accepted without comment.


Expected
pnpm parity in both directions: a frozen install fails on a patch-content/hash mismatch the way pnpm does, and a plain install that applies changed patch content recomputes the hash and updates the lockfile in the same pass.
Real-world context
Hit immediately downstream of #1195: after hand-repairing the combined patch file, no install ever updated or flagged the recorded hash, so local CI=1 installs stayed green while the same tree would fail any native-pnpm frozen CI. In a repo shared between aube and pnpm users, the desync is invisible to the aube side and breaking for the pnpm side.
Related: #1195 / #1196 (patch-commit layering), #1029 (re-resolve dropped pnpm patch metadata)."},{"number":1195,"title":"`aube patch-commit` on an already-patched package emits an incremental diff that can never apply, breaking install","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1195","updatedAt":"2026-08-01T20:33:33Z","bodyText":"aube: 1.36.0 linux-x64 (2026-07-29)
Repro: https://github.com/mwolson/tmp-aube-issues/tree/main/pnpm-patch-commit-existing-patch (./repro.sh exits non-zero while the issue reproduces)

Setup
A workspace with one dependency that already has a declared patch:
# pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
  - .
patchedDependencies:
  "@isaacs/string-locale-compare@1.1.0": patches/@isaacs__string-locale-compare@1.1.0.patch
The existing patch adds one marker line to index.js. aube install applies it fine.
Steps
aube install --ignore-scripts
aube patch @isaacs/string-locale-compare@1.1.0
# append one line to <edit-dir>/index.js
aube patch-commit <edit-dir>
The extract half behaves correctly: the edit folder contains the package with the existing patch applied, which is the right baseline for layering an edit (matches pnpm).
What happens
patch-commit then does three things wrong at once:


It diffs the edit folder against the already-patched baseline rather than the pristine tarball, so the emitted patch contains only the new hunks, with line numbers and context from the patched file:
diff --git a/index.js b/index.js
--- a/index.js
+++ b/index.js
@@ -42,3 +42,5 @@
 }

 // aube-repro original patch marker
+
+// aube-repro second patch marker


It writes that diff to a new file, patches/@isaacs+string-locale-compare@1.1.0.patch, and repoints pnpm-workspace.yaml at it. The original patches/@isaacs__string-locale-compare@1.1.0.patch is left orphaned on disk, and its content is no longer referenced anywhere — the first patch's changes are effectively dropped from the declaration.


The immediate relink then fails, because the incremental hunks cannot apply to the pristine package:
× failed to link workspace node_modules
╰─▶ failed to apply patch for @isaacs/string-locale-compare@1.1.0: failed to
    apply patch for index.js: error applying hunk #1

Every subsequent aube install fails the same way, so the project stays broken until the workspace entry and patch file are restored by hand.


Expected
pnpm parity for the same flow: patch-commit after an extract that included the existing patch emits a combined patch against the pristine package, and updates the already-declared patch path in place rather than minting a second file. (The @scope+name vs pnpm's @scope__name naming for newly created patch files is harmless by itself since the declaration carries the path, but here it compounds the confusion because both files end up on disk.)
Hit in a real workspace while layering a second hunk onto an existing patch for @legendapp/list; recovery meant rebuilding the combined patch by hand from the pristine tarball plus both diffs and restoring the workspace entry.
Related: #383 noted patch-commit previously writing the declaration to package.json instead of pnpm-workspace.yaml — that part works now; this is the neighboring case where the declaration target is right but the diff baseline and file identity are not."},{"number":1204,"title":"Add license information to SBOM (CycloneDX) outputs","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1204","updatedAt":"2026-08-01T17:37:53Z","bodyText":"Currently, when one runs aube sbom, it generates a CycloneDX SBOM where components entries don't have the licenses files:

I'm using the default minimumReleaseAge."},{"number":1083,"title":"Embedder support for wrapping the Node runtime (not just selecting one)","url":"https://github.com/aubepkg/aube/discussions/1083","updatedAt":"2026-07-30T16:16:22Z","bodyText":"PR #1079 lets an embedder point aube at a Node for lifecycle scripts — a version manager selecting a toolchain. It can't express an embedder that wraps Node rather than selecting one: an instrumenting runtime, a transpiling loader, a sandbox. That case needs three things the current hook doesn't carry.

Three independent paths, not one. Today node_bin_dir becomes the PATH entry, NODE, and npm_node_execpath at once (node_bin = bin_dir.join("node")). A wrapper needs them distinct: its shim dir on PATH, NODE at the shim so $NODE child.js in a script stays wrapped, and npm_node_execpath at the real node, which node-gyp and native-addon tooling read to find Node's install prefix.
A lifecycle-script env contribution. For a wrapper the environment is the mechanism: a NODE_OPTIONS preload is how you interpose without patching Node. There's no hook for it today.
Every spawn path, not just the install scope. The seed_embedder_node hook only applies inside runtime::scope, so dlx/exec/run/node never see it. A selector that misses a path falls back to the ambient node; a wrapper silently runs dependencies unwrapped, which is worse than not wrapping.

The proposal is to let an embedder describe a Node invocation rather than a bin dir:
pub struct EmbedderRuntime {
    pub bin_dir: Option<PathBuf>,        // PATH entry; need not contain `node`
    pub node_program: Option<PathBuf>,   // `NODE` and the spawn program; None => bin_dir.join(node)
    pub node_execpath: Option<PathBuf>,  // `npm_node_execpath`; None => node_program
    pub version: Option<String>,         // supplied, not probed
    pub env: Vec<(OsString, OsString)>,  // applied last to every lifecycle spawn
}
Embedder side. The host resolves its own runtime, then describes how Node should be invoked — per call, or registered once so every spawn path sees it:
let runtime = EmbedderRuntime {
    bin_dir: Some(shim_dir.clone()),         // …/shim — on PATH, holds the wrapper `node`
    node_execpath: Some(real_node.clone()),  // …/node-24.4.1/bin/node — the real binary
    version: Some("24.4.1".into()),
    env: vec![("NODE_OPTIONS".into(), "--import /…/preload.mjs".into())],
    ..Default::default()                     // node_program defaults to bin_dir/node
};

// Per call, as #1079 does today.
aube::embed::install(InstallOptions { runtime: Some(runtime.clone()), ..opts }).await?;

// Or once at startup, so dlx / exec / run / node are covered too.
aube::embed::set_embedder_runtime(runtime);
Script side. A dependency's postinstall then runs with:
PATH=/…/shim:/…/node_modules/.bin:…
NODE=/…/shim/node
npm_node_execpath=/…/node-24.4.1/bin/node
NODE_OPTIONS=--import /…/preload.mjs
Each of these then does the right thing:
node build.js        # resolves through PATH to the shim, so it runs wrapped
"$NODE" build.js     # same, for a script that re-spawns explicitly
node-gyp rebuild     # builds against npm_node_execpath, the real Node
Every field is optional and unset reproduces today's behavior, so standalone aube is unchanged. The existing node_bin_dir becomes the degenerate case ({ bin_dir }). Registration is set-once and first-write-wins, the same shape as set_embedder / set_embedder_defaults, with a per-call value taking precedence, so the ambient path costs no mutable runtime global.

AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/unavailable; version: unavailable."},{"number":12709,"title":"Proposal: give every Omarchy user a declarative "my machine" file with `mise bootstrap`","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12709","updatedAt":"2026-09-04T19:08:19Z","bodyText":"Omarchy already ships mise, and as of the lazy-tools change it declares its default agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, gh, opencode, and the rest) as lazy tools in a system-level mise config at /etc/mise/config.toml. That file is already a small "Omarchy layer": it says what the distro wants on the machine, and a user's own ~/.config/mise/config.toml layers on top of it, so pinning claude to a version in the global config already overrides Omarchy's latest.
mise has a second half that Omarchy is not using yet: mise bootstrap, which converges a machine to a declared state. Packages, system files, systemd services, firewall rules, dotfiles, and the tools it already handles. It uses the same config files and the same layering. I maintain mise, and I am willing to make broad changes to bootstrap to fit Omarchy. This post is about what extending that existing layer would give Omarchy users that they do not have today.
The user problem
Omarchy makes a fresh machine beautiful in twenty minutes. Then people spend the next month making it theirs: pacman -S a dozen things, remove the preinstalls they never open, flip a service, tweak a Hyprland file, install their language toolchains. None of that is recorded anywhere. When they get a second machine, reinstall after a bad experiment, or move from the laptop to a desktop, they do it all again from memory.
The current answer is "keep notes" or "write a shell script". Neither is Omarchy-grade.
This is opt-in
Nothing here is required to set up or use an Omarchy machine. The installer, omarchy update, and every existing command keep working exactly as they do for someone who never touches a mise config. Bootstrap is one way to make a setup trackable and shareable for the people who want that. Users who prefer to pacman -S things by hand lose nothing.
What it would look like
The user's global mise config, ~/.config/mise/config.toml, becomes the one file that describes their machine. ~/.config/mise is a git checkout, so that file and the dotfiles next to it live in a repo. Roughly:
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml

# Extra packages on top of Omarchy
[bootstrap.packages]
"pacman:helix" = "latest"
"pacman:zathura" = "latest"
"pacman:libreoffice-fresh" = { state = "absent" }   # a preinstall, gone (not in mise yet, see below)

# Flip an Omarchy default
[bootstrap.services.cups]
enabled = false
state = "stopped"

# Dev toolchains. This is the same [tools] table `mise use -g` already writes to,
# and the same table Omarchy's /etc/mise/config.toml uses for its lazy agent CLIs.
[tools]
node = "lts"
ruby = "latest"
rust = "latest"
claude = "2.1"          # overrides Omarchy's lazy `latest`, works today

# Their own config files, kept in the same repo and symlinked into place
[dotfiles]
"~/.config/hypr/bindings.lua" = "hypr/bindings.lua"
"~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.toml" = "alacritty/alacritty.toml"
"~/.gitconfig" = "gitconfig"
On a fresh Omarchy machine:
omarchy setup dotfiles git@github.com:me/omarchy-setup.git
which checks the repo out as ~/.config/mise and runs mise bootstrap. Ten minutes later it is their machine. From then on omarchy update runs plain mise bootstrap, so declared packages and files stay applied over time. There is no separate dotfiles repo path for Omarchy to remember, because the global config is the repo.
What users get that they do not have today
Their setup gets recorded without them doing anything new. Because the repo is the global config, every mise use -g node a user already runs today lands in the repo. Omarchy's own dev-env installer writes there too. Add omarchy pkg add delegating to mise bootstrap packages use -g pacman:... and installing a package records it as well. The declared file stays true because the tools people already use write to it.
Reinstall stops being scary. A fresh Omarchy install plus one command gets someone back to their exact setup. That makes people far more willing to try things, wipe, and start over, which is the mindset Omarchy wants to encourage.
Many machines, one source of truth. Laptop and desktop share the repo. mise environments (-E work, -E home) handle the differences from one config.
Customizing Omarchy by declaring, not by fighting it. Today the only Omarchy default a user can override declaratively is a tool version. Removing a preinstall or disabling a default service is a manual action Omarchy might undo on the next refresh, and the preinstalls toggle works by deleting and reinstalling the whole system mise file. With bootstrap, the same override mechanism that already works for tools covers packages, services, and files. I verified this week that a user config overriding a system-level declaration works today: the plan showed the union of both, the user's entries won on shared keys, and each line named the config that declared it.
A machine that can tell you what changed. mise bootstrap plan and mise bootstrap status --missing are a drift report. "Why is my machine different from my other one" has an answer.
Shareable setups. "Omarchy, but set up for Rails work" or "Omarchy for a Framework 13 in a design shop" becomes a repo someone can fork. That is a community surface Omarchy does not have.
Fleets, later. The same config applies to other machines with mise bootstrap remote, which stages the project over plain OpenSSH and runs bootstrap there. Hosts live in an inventory with tags, and -E environments give a host its profile, so this is the Ansible shape without Python on the target. Nobody needs this to set up one laptop. It matters when a team, a classroom, or a company wants ten Omarchy machines to match one repo, and it means Omarchy would not have to build its own fleet story when that comes up.
Agents can edit TOML safely. Omarchy's pitch is Beautiful, Fun and Agentic. An agent adding a package by editing one declared file and running plan is a much safer loop than an agent running sudo pacman -S. The desired state is reviewable in a diff before anything happens, and it is already in git.
What Omarchy itself gets
This is secondary, but real. A good share of install/config/ and of the migrations are hand-written versions of "ensure this service is enabled", "ensure this file is in /etc with these permissions", "ensure this package is present". Those become [bootstrap.*] sections next to the [tools] table Omarchy already ships in /etc/mise/config.toml (or a sibling file in /etc/mise/conf.d/), converged on every update, with no marker files and no bespoke idempotency logic per script. The user's global config layers on top of that system file, which is exactly why the user story above works and why the tool-version override works already.
What does not work yet, and what I will build
I want to be straight about the gaps, because they are mine to fix.

Declarative package removal. Today state = "absent" for a pacman package does not exist. It is the most common customization after "add these", so it is first.
AUR. The pacman backend does not build AUR packages. Omarchy has AUR packages, and users will ask.
Checking a repo out as the global config. mise bootstrap --from <url> exists but clones to a side directory. It should be able to make the checkout ~/.config/mise itself, with sane handling of an existing config there.
An enable-only mode for services and firewall. The Omarchy installer runs in a chroot with no live systemd and must not enable UFW live. Bootstrap needs a mode that writes enable symlinks and rules without starting anything, so the same declarations can run at install time and on the installed system.
Anything else Omarchy needs. If adopting this surfaces a rough edge in mise, I would rather change mise than have Omarchy work around it in bash.

On the Omarchy side the main thing to sort out is omarchy-refresh-config, which copies onto the target and would write through a symlink into a user's repo. That is a small change once the model is agreed.
Proposed order

Add [bootstrap.services] and [bootstrap.files] declarations beside the existing lazy [tools] in Omarchy's system mise config, and apply them from omarchy update and omarchy-migrate. No user-facing surface yet. This proves the model on the file that already exists.
Add omarchy setup dotfiles, run mise bootstrap from omarchy update, and point omarchy pkg add at the declared config. Small once step 1 exists.
Land package removal, AUR, global-config checkout, and enable-only mode in mise in parallel, then extend the installer to use the same declarations.

I am happy to do the mise work and to help with the Omarchy side. Interested in whether this direction appeals before writing any code."},{"number":12359,"title":"Mise tasks conflicts with `pyproject.toml` in sub folder","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12359","updatedAt":"2026-09-07T07:12:54Z","bodyText":"While working on a project where we use mise tasks quite a bit, I ran into an issue when making one of the tasks a minimal Python task with locked dependencies.

I've tried using .miserc.toml in the root of the project to ignore the pyproject.toml file, but I was unsuccessful."},{"number":12756,"title":"bootstrap plan: report declared non-composed surfaces across config_roots (read-only)","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12756","updatedAt":"2026-09-04T12:24:59Z","bodyText":"Context: #12099 shipped selected-root composition for [dotfiles], [bootstrap.files], [bootstrap.directories], [bootstrap.services], and [bootstrap.compose] (#12100 provenance, #12105/#12132 composition, #12190 disjoint symlink-each). Verified in production: a dotfiles repo driving config_roots = ["bundles/*"] with 30+ sibling roots now converges the declarative surfaces in a single composed pass.
The gap: packages, repos, accounts, and hooks stay per-root by design — the docs say to "use their existing explicit workflows when those resources need aggregate behavior". Those workflows need to know which roots declare what before running per-root passes, and today the only way to find out is re-parsing TOML outside mise.
What a multi-root repo does today (from my init task):
for dir in bundles/*/; do
  if grep -qsE '^\[bootstrap\.(packages|repos|users|groups)|^(pre|post)-(packages|repos) = |^final = ' \
     "$dir"mise.toml "$dir"mise.*.toml 2>/dev/null; then
    (cd "$dir" && mise bootstrap --yes --skip-dirty --only accounts,packages,repos,final-hook)
  fi
done
That regex re-implements config discovery mise already owns, and it breaks on TOML shapes the regex did not anticipate (inline tables, multiline arrays, quoted keys). It also cannot see which env-specific configs are active per root — the monorepo loader already computes exactly that.
Proposal — read-only collection, no execution
mise bootstrap plan --config-roots "bundles/*" [--json]
# per matched root: which non-composed bootstrap surfaces are declared,
# with #12100 provenance (declaring config, config_root, active envs)
JSON sketch:
{
  "roots": [
    {
      "config_root": "bundles/deepgram",
      "envs": ["exe.xyz"],
      "declares": {
        "packages": { "count": 3, "provenance": "bundles/deepgram/mise.toml" },
        "repos":    { "count": 1, "provenance": "bundles/deepgram/mise.toml" },
        "accounts": { "count": 0 },
        "hooks":    ["post-packages", "final"]
      }
    }
  ]
}
Deliberately out of scope (why this stays small)

nothing executes — no sudo, no network, no ordering questions;
nothing merges — tables stay per-root, so the hierarchical-precedence concern from #12099 does not apply;
no lifecycle contract for hooks — they are reported, not run.

What it unblocks

structural discovery — the grep leaves the init task entirely;
cross-root drift checks with --detailed-exitcode-style semantics, hookable from CI;
a natural follow-up to discuss separately: explicit fan-out execution, e.g. mise bootstrap --config-roots "bundles/*" --only accounts,packages,repos — iteration over roots, not composition of their tables.

Verified against 2026.9.1: bootstrap plan covers declarative resources only and takes no --config-roots flag. The collection half looks like mostly output shaping, since the monorepo loader already discovers each root's active env-specific configs.
Happy to take a stab at a PR if the shape sounds right."},{"number":12761,"title":"task cache audit: a strace ptrace failure fails the task, although the audit is advisory","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12761","updatedAt":"2026-09-04T12:02:20Z","bodyText":"Summary
With cache = { enabled = true, audit = true } on Linux, mise runs the task under strace. When strace itself fails mid-run with
/usr/bin/strace: ptrace(PTRACE_LISTEN,pid:5359,sig:0): Input/output error

the task is reported as failed:
ERROR 1 task(s) failed:
[//gitops:test] exited with status 1
[//gitops:test] ERROR task failed

although every test inside it passed (the suite's own output shows only ✔ lines). The docs say the audit "is advisory, reporting relative paths without blocking tasks or preventing caching", so a failure inside the audit wrapper should degrade to "audit unavailable" (a warning, no report) and leave the task's own exit status in charge.
Environment

mise 2026.8.10 (our CI pin; I found no change in the release notes up to v2026.9.1 that touches this)
Linux, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, strace from the runner image (/usr/bin/strace)
Task: a node --test suite that spawns many short-lived child processes (git, helm, yq)

Frequency
Across roughly 1,100 strace-wrapped task executions in our CI over nine days we saw the same ptrace(PTRACE_LISTEN …): Input/output error five times, three in a dedicated audit job and twice in ordinary test jobs. It is a race in ptrace on a busy runner, not a property of the task: the same task passes on re-run every time. Because audit = true is a per-task setting, every job that runs the task traces it, including jobs that never read the report, so the flake reaches required checks.
Expected
The audit reports what it could trace, or reports nothing with a warning, and the task's exit status decides success. An operator who wants a broken trace to fail a run can detect it from the missing report (we already do that in the audit job by grepping the log for strace:).
Actual
The task fails with the wrapper's exit status, so an advisory feature fails a required CI gate.
Suggestions

Do not inherit strace's exit status: if the tracer dies, log a warning, skip the report, and use the task's own status.
A run-level switch to disable the audit (MISE_TASK_CACHE_AUDIT=false / --task-cache-audit=off, or tracing only when task.cache.audit_report is set), so jobs that do not consume the report do not pay the tracing overhead or its failure modes. Today audit is only settable per task in mise.toml."},{"number":12763,"title":"`[bootstrap.files].source` does not expand `~`, while `[dotfiles].source` does","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12763","updatedAt":"2026-09-04T12:01:43Z","bodyText":"[dotfiles].source expands a leading ~. [bootstrap.files].source treats it
as a literal path segment and joins it onto the config file's directory, so the
read fails.
Repro
mkdir -p /tmp/repro/home/.config/mise /tmp/repro/home/src
printf 'hello\n' > /tmp/repro/home/src/file.txt
cat > /tmp/repro/home/.config/mise/config.toml <<'EOF'
[dotfiles]
"~/.via-dotfiles" = { source = "~/src/file.txt", mode = "symlink" }

[bootstrap.files."~/.via-files"]
source = "~/src/file.txt"
EOF
export HOME=/tmp/repro/home
mise trust "$HOME/.config/mise/config.toml"
mise bootstrap dotfiles status   # accepts the source
mise bootstrap files status      # fails on the same string
~/.via-dotfiles  symlink  ~/src/file.txt  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  missing

mise ERROR [bootstrap.files]."/tmp/repro/home/.via-files": failed to read source /tmp/repro/home/.config/mise/~/src/file.txt
mise ERROR No such file or directory (os error 2)

Applying the [dotfiles] entry confirms the expansion is real: the link points
at /tmp/repro/home/src/file.txt.
Expected
[bootstrap.files] and [bootstrap.directories] accept ~ the way
[dotfiles].source does. Both fields name a source file the same way.
Cause
resolve_source_path in src/system/managed_files.rs is absolute-or-join with
no expansion, and base is cf.get_path().parent(). So $HOME and template
braces are literal there too, while absolute and relative paths both work.
Secondary ask
My global config is symlinked into a dotfiles repo, and the relative base is the
symlink's directory rather than the target's, so those sources carry absolute
/Users/<me>/... paths. config_source (#12454) would express it exactly, but
these fields are not templated at all. That is #9100
Please leave the relative base as it is: canonicalizing it would silently move
every existing relative source behind a symlinked config.

Tested on nushell v0.115.1 and mise v2026.9.0 and v2026.9.1."},{"number":12747,"title":"oci push --cache-from bakes wrong PATH for a reused tool layer without a bin/ subdir (e.g. pnpm via aqua)","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12747","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T21:37:33Z","bodyText":"Summary
mise oci push --cache-from <ref> reuses a tool's layer when (tool, version, mount point, owner) match the cache-from image, skipping a local install for that tool. The reused layer's files are correct, but the image's baked PATH for that tool is wrong when the tool's real install layout isn't <install>/bin — the reuse path appears to fall back to that generic assumption instead of the backend's actual list_bin_paths result, which is only computed when the tool is installed locally.
Confirmed with pnpm (resolves to the aqua backend, aqua:pnpm/pnpm, by default), which installs the binary directly at the install root — list_bin_paths reports [<install_dir>], no bin/. A push that installs pnpm locally bakes the correct PATH; a push that reuses the same tool+version from --cache-from without installing bakes <install_dir>/bin, which doesn't exist.
Environment

mise 2026.8.2 (linux-x64)
oci feature, settings.experimental = true

Minimal repro
# mise.toml
[settings]
experimental = true

[tools]
pnpm = "9.15.9"

[tasks.repro]
tools.crane = "latest"
tools.pitchfork = "latest"
tools.jq = "latest"
run = '''
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

pitchfork run reg --expected-port 41234 -- crane registry serve
img="localhost:41234/repro"

mise install -y pnpm@9.15.9
mise oci push -y "$img:v1"

mise uninstall -y pnpm@9.15.9
mise oci push -y --cache-from "$img:v1" "$img:v2"

echo "\n== v1 image, pushed with pnpm installed, no registry cache"
crane config "$img:v1" | jq -r '.config.Env[] | select(startswith("PATH="))'
echo "\n== v2 image, pushed without pnpm installed, cache from v1"
crane config "$img:v2" | jq -r '.config.Env[] | select(startswith("PATH="))'

pitchfork stop reg
'''
mise trust && mise run repro
Actual output
== v1 image, pushed with pnpm installed, no cache
PATH=/mise/installs/pnpm/9.15.9:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

== v2 image, pushed without pnpm installed, cache from v1
PATH=/mise/installs/pnpm/9.15.9/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

Same tool, same version, same layer content (--cache-from reused it) — only the baked PATH differs, and only the reused-without-install one is wrong.
Expected
A reused layer's baked PATH/exec_env should match what installing that exact tool+version locally would produce.
Suggested fix
Persist the tool's derived exec_env as a layer annotation when first computed from a real local install — alongside the existing dev.mise.layer.prefix / dev.mise.layer.owner cache-key annotations (#11142) — so reuse restores the real env instead of falling back to a generic default. Short of that: warn in mise oci push output when reusing a layer whose backend's exec_env can't be derived without a local install, and/or add a scoped --no-cache-for <tool> so callers don't have to give up layer reuse for every tool just to route around one.
Workaround in use for now
Not trusting the image's baked PATH for pnpm; resolving it via mise which pnpm / mise exec at container runtime instead, since the actual installed files are present and correct there — only the precomputed PATH string baked at push time is wrong."},{"number":12744,"title":"Custom backend stopped installing after update","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12744","updatedAt":"2026-09-04T00:45:21Z","bodyText":"Hi,

The program works fine, but it produces paths that are incompatible with GitBash. Any command that updates the PATH variable (including eval $(mise activate bash)) corrupts the GitBash terminal session, rendering it unusable because GitBash cannot find any commands anymore due to the corrupted PATH variable.
The problem:
mise outputs paths in Windows format: C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\bin;C:\Program Files\Git\usr\local\bin;C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin using the C: prefix, the \ directory separator, and the ; path separator. However, GitBash expects paths to be in Linux format: using /c/ prefix, / directory separator, and : path separator.
One element of solution:
When running under GitBash ($OSTYPE == "msys"), paths generated by mise should be in Linux format using the / and : separators. In addition, paths pointing to directories inside the GitBash installation directory should be without the C:\Program Files\Git prefix, so that they are seen as absolute paths inside the Linux VFS. For example, C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\bin => /mingw64/bin, C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin => /usr/bin."},{"number":12734,"title":"Allow `mise self-update` to source releases from a private repo or a custom manifest (org-governed distribution)","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12734","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T12:54:07Z","bodyText":"Context
We're evaluating adopting mise as our organization's standard tool version manager. One open question in that evaluation is how to govern mise self-update itself: today it always talks to jdx/mise on api.github.com, so there's no way for an organization to control which mise versions are safe to roll out before they land on developer machines and CI runners.
We looked at the existing options (.disable-self-update marker, mise-self-update-instructions.toml, MISE_SELF_UPDATE_AVAILABLE=false) — these are great for "point people somewhere else" but they only show a message; they don't give mise an actual alternate source of truth for "what versions are approved". Without that, an org's options are either (a) fully disable self-update and lose the convenience entirely, or (b) leave it pointed at upstream and hope nothing lands that breaks a pipeline before anyone notices.
This is adjacent to #8008, which asks for self-update to use mise-versions.jdx.dev instead of hitting GitHub directly — same root cause (the update source is hardcoded), different motivation (rate limits vs. governance).
Proposal
Make the release source mise self-update talks to configurable, for two concrete shapes an org is likely to use:

A private repo on github.com (a fork/mirror an org curates — merges in only the upstream releases it has vetted).
A custom artifact host that requires auth (Artifactory, Nexus, an internal S3 bucket, a plain static file server, …) — for orgs that don't want to depend on GitHub at all for internal tooling distribution.

Why this is smaller than it might sound
mise already depends on the self_update crate (currently pinned to a recent 1.x — see #12714), and that crate already ships both extension points needed here; self_update.rs just doesn't wire them up yet:

UpdateBuilder::api_base_url — already documented for "e.g. for a github enterprise installation", but works for any GitHub-API-shaped host, including a plain private repo on api.github.com itself (no GHE needed — same host, different owner/repo).

Private repos already work end-to-end with the existing flow: the crate's GitHub backend resolves each asset's download URL from the API's url field (the authenticated /releases/assets/{id} endpoint), not browser_download_url, and "the download path applies the same auth-header derivation the listing path uses" (from the crate's own docs). So once repo_owner/repo_name are configurable, a private repo just needs a token with read access — no new auth plumbing, mise's existing GitHub token resolution chain (env vars, credential_command, github_tokens.toml, gh CLI's hosts.yml, git credential helpers) already covers it.


backends::manifest — a ready-made backend (crate feature manifest, not yet enabled in mise's Cargo.toml) for "any plain file server ... that serves a single JSON document describing your releases": you publish a small manifest.json (schema + list of {version, assets: [{name, url, digest}]}) next to your binaries, no server-side API needed. Its builder shares the same request_header(...) / http_client(...) / add_root_certificate(...) setters every other backend has, applied to both the manifest fetch and the asset download — which is exactly what's needed to carry an Artifactory API key, a bearer token, or mTLS.

So this isn't "build a new update mechanism" — it's "expose configuration for two things the dependency already does", roughly in the spirit of how github: tool backends already expose api_url for enterprise hosts.
Sketch of what this could look like
[settings.self_update]
# Option A: point at a different github.com (or GHE) repo
repo = "myorg/mise-mirror"

# Option B: point at a manifest-based source instead
manifest_url = "https://artifactory.mycorp.com/generic-mise/manifest.json"

# Credential for either option, resolved the same way github.credential_command works today
credential_command = "vault read -field=token secret/mise-self-update"
Fully opt-in — the default stays exactly as today (jdx/mise on api.github.com, unauthenticated or using the existing GitHub token chain).
Open questions

Should this live under [settings.self_update], or be folded into the existing github.* settings namespace?
For the manifest path, does mise want a single generic credential_command, or mirror the request_header-style flexibility directly (name/value pairs in config)?
Is there any appetite for this at all, or is the intended answer for org governance "disable self-update entirely and distribute mise through your own package manager"? We'd rather find that out here before attempting a PR, per the contributing guide.

Happy to put together a PR once there's rough agreement on shape — wanted to raise this as a discussion first since it touches the update mechanism's trust model."},{"number":12730,"title":"Private Go modules cannot be resolved with @latest","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12730","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T10:55:56Z","bodyText":"I’m trying to install a private Go CLI using mise’s Go backend:
mise use --global "go:github.com/example-org/private-cli@latest"
The module is hosted in a private GitHub repository and has regular semver tags. GOPRIVATE and GitHub authentication are configured correctly.
The command fails with:
mise WARN  No versions found for go:github.com/example-org/private-cli
mise ERROR ... no versions found ... matching date filter

Installing a concrete version works:
mise use --global "go:github.com/example-org/private-cli@v1.2.3"
The same problem occurs for a CLI package nested below the module root, for example:
github.com/example-org/private-cli/cmd/tool

On a clean cache, mise appears to fall back to VCS-based discovery after the public proxy returns 404. It then fetches metadata for every tag, exceeding mise’s default 20-second
fetch_remote_versions_timeout. Increasing the timeout may mask the symptom, but does not address the expensive discovery path.
A possible direction for a fix could be:

Make discovery use the effective mise environment, including GOPRIVATE and GOPROXY.
Avoid querying the public proxy for paths matching GOPPRIVATE/GONOPROXY.
Use Go-native @latest resolution for private modules.
For nested packages, walk module-path prefixes and resolve @latest on the actual module root.
Fetch metadata for every version only when a date-based filter requires it.

This is only a proposed direction and I’d appreciate feedback on whether it fits mise’s architecture, or whether there is a better way to support private Go CLIs."},{"number":12733,"title":"mise became too talkative lately?!?","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12733","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T10:43:22Z","bodyText":"mise rocks! it replaced most of my homebrew setup. that said, it got a little too talkative lately for my taste.

personally, i'd prefer mise to let me specify a --verbose option, and otherwise stay calm. do not make me read unnecessary stuff."},{"number":12681,"title":"bootstrap systemd units: support environment_file, nice, umask, requires","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12681","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T09:39:36Z","bodyText":"I manage a four-machine fleet (two Ubuntu, two macOS) with mise bootstrap as the config spine — [bootstrap.linux.systemd.units] and [bootstrap.macos.launchd.agents] declare every scheduled job, which replaced a pile of hand-written unit renderers. It works well; thank you for building it.
While porting existing systemd services into the table I hit four standard unit directives that the schema doesn't carry yet. Against 2026.9.0 they're accepted with an unknown field warning and discarded:



Proposed TOML key
systemd directive
Why it comes up




environment_file
EnvironmentFile=
The standard pattern for keeping credentials/env out of the unit file itself; most existing services that read a token use it. The workaround (sh -c '. file; exec …' in exec_start) works but loses systemd's - optional-file semantics and makes the exec line lie about what runs.


nice
Nice=
Background maintenance jobs (sweeps, reindexing) that shouldn't compete with interactive work. Currently expressible only by prefixing /usr/bin/nice -n … in exec_start.


umask
UMask=
Services writing files a group shares. No clean exec-line workaround since the wrapping shell's umask isn't the service's.


requires
Requires=
Hard dependencies, where after + wants (already supported) deliberately express something weaker.



All four are 1:1 passthroughs in the same shape as the existing supported-keys table, so they'd inherit the current docs/validation pattern rather than needing new machinery. I'd expect anyone migrating pre-existing units into the table to hit environment_file almost immediately; the other three are rarer but each appeared within one real fleet's dozen services.
Happy to open a PR for these if the direction sounds right — the field-mapping code looks mechanical to extend, and I'd follow the existing table's style."},{"number":12722,"title":"`mise plugins list` lacks docs for `--core` and `--user` flags","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12722","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T21:53:14Z","bodyText":"The -c, --core and --user flags are only documented for mise plugins, but not for mise plugins list command, though they are accepted by and meaningful to the latter command.

I know it's a contrived scenario but I think it gets the point across.
I want to author an addition to mise, in the form of a new command mise vendor (or a sub-command under mise generate). The rough idea is that mise vendor will take the packages in your mise.lock and will download the installation sources (i.e .tar.gz etc) from whatever backend the tool comes from, and save it locally. Then users may back up the vendored directory however they see fit.
When restoring from a vendored backup, mise will use the local vendored sources to install the tools it is requesting, and will seamlessly switch back over to using whatever original remote backend the tools actually came from when updating the tool.
Necessary changes:

Add the mise vendor command

Download installation sources and save them locally
Manifest of local vendored sources & hashes for provenance,verification & other security concerns


extend mise generate bootstrap to allow the mise bootstrap script to use a local archive of mise, instead of downloading from github

mise vendor will use it to vendor mise itself


a vendored backend which will report that it provides the vendored tools at their specific revision, with a high priority so that install/use will first use the vendored backend before trying any other backends.

Or a mise vendor restore (name TBD) command that acts as the only way to use the aforementioned vendored backend.
I'm pretty sure I can implement this backend as a backend plugin in Lua, which I will do as a Proof of Concept



I'm not super attached to the proposed names of commands/things I gave in this summary, they names are just to communicate the idea and the concepts used, that is to say I'm happy to take suggestions or directives about names."},{"number":12719,"title":"Zsh completion for `mise plugins uninstall` only lists core plugins","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12719","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T21:44:26Z","bodyText":"$ mise plugin

A task with sources globs and cache = { enabled = true } hashes its sources by expanding the glob. The ** expansion follows symlinks and has no loop detection. On a tree that links back into itself, mise allocates until it is killed and the task command never runs.
Reproduction steps:
[settings]
experimental = true

# Two links are the smallest trigger, because the Linux kernel stops a single loop at 40 levels (ELOOP).
[tasks.make-loop-tree]
description = "Sets up 2 sym links in a loop."
run = "mkdir -p tree && ln -sfn . tree/a && ln -sfn . tree/b"

[tasks.cached-task]
depends = ["make-loop-tree"]
run = "true"
sources = ["tree/**/*"]
outputs = []
cache = { enabled = true }

[tasks.cached-task-watched]
description = "Runs cached-task in the background, prints its memory usage once a second, and kills it past MEMORY_LIMIT_MB."
quiet = true
run = """
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u

memory_limit_mb=${MEMORY_LIMIT_MB:-1024}
timeout_seconds=60

mise run cached-task &
mise_pid=$!

elapsed_seconds=0
while kill -0 "$mise_pid" 2>/dev/null && [ "$elapsed_seconds" -lt "$timeout_seconds" ]; do
  sleep 1
  elapsed_seconds=$((elapsed_seconds + 1))

  rss_kb=$(ps -o rss= -p "$mise_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
  rss_mb=$(( ${rss_kb:-0} / 1024 ))
  echo "after ${elapsed_seconds}s: mise is using ${rss_mb} MB"

  if [ "$rss_mb" -gt "$memory_limit_mb" ]; then
    kill -9 "$mise_pid"
    echo "killed mise at ${rss_mb} MB. The task command never ran."
    exit 1
  fi
done

wait "$mise_pid"
"""

Save mise.toml in an empty directory, then:
mise trust && mise run cached-task-watched

Without the watched command, mise run cached-task, grows by 50 to 100 MB per second until the OS kills it.

I ran into this issue when I added test fixtures to my application for reading hardware sensors on Linux. sysfs links each device to its class in both directions: class/hwmon/hwmon0 points at the device directory, and the device's subsystem points back at class/hwmon."},{"number":12690,"title":"Lazy tools do not work on Windows","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12690","updatedAt":"2026-09-02T15:11:35Z","bodyText":"Using mise version 2026.09.0 on Windows.

The docs state that setting an env var to
false clears it:
[env]
NODE_ENV = false # unset a previously set NODE_ENV
In practice false only cancels an assignment made by an earlier mise config
file. If the variable already exists in the process environment when mise runs,
it survives untouched and leaks into mise exec, mise run, mise env and
activated shells.
The same docs page establishes that mise reasons about this state elsewhere — the
default directive is described as keeping a value "if it was already set
before mise ran or by an earlier config file" — so false failing to reach
the pre-existing case reads as a bug rather than intended scoping.
Reproduction
A single mise.toml, nothing else:
[env]
FOO = false
$ mise exec -- sh -c 'echo ${FOO-<absent>}'
<absent>                # correct

$ FOO=leaked mise exec -- sh -c 'echo ${FOO-<absent>}'
leaked                  # BUG: expected <absent>
${FOO-<absent>} is deliberate — plain $FOO cannot distinguish "set to the
empty string" from "genuinely unset", which is what made this hard to spot.
Reproduced in a fully clean environment, with mise never activated, to rule out
any session state:
$ env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin FOO=leaked \
      /usr/local/bin/mise -C /tmp/repro exec -- sh -c 'echo FOO=[${FOO-<absent>}]'
FOO=[leaked]
Affected surfaces
Every surface leaks. The commands below use a slightly larger config than the one
above: a profile, plus a second variable as a control, plus a task.
# mise.toml
[env]
SET_ENV = 'set'
UNSET_ENV = 'unset'

[tasks]
check = "echo SET_ENV=[${SET_ENV-<absent>}] UNSET_ENV=[${UNSET_ENV-<absent>}]"
# mise.dev.toml
[env]
UNSET_ENV = false
SET_ENV = 'dev'
$ mise run check
SET_ENV=[set] UNSET_ENV=[unset]

$ MISE_ENV=dev mise run check
SET_ENV=[dev] UNSET_ENV=[<absent>]              # correct

$ UNSET_ENV=from_parent MISE_ENV=dev mise run check
SET_ENV=[dev] UNSET_ENV=[from_parent]           # BUG
With UNSET_ENV=from_parent MISE_ENV=dev:



Surface
Result
Expected




mise exec -- sh -c 'echo ${UNSET_ENV-<absent>}'
from_parent
<absent>


mise run check
from_parent
<absent>


mise env -s bash
no unset line emitted
unset UNSET_ENV


mise env --json
key absent from output
n/a (cannot express an unset)


mise activate bash + _mise_hook
from_parent
<absent>


mise hook-env -s bash
UNSET_ENV not mentioned
unset UNSET_ENV



Note the SET_ENV control in the same runs: overriding a pre-existing value with
a string works correctly (from_parent → dev). Only the false / unset path
fails.
The activated-shell row, from a clean shell:
$ env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin \
      UNSET_ENV=from_parent MISE_ENV=dev \
      bash --noprofile --norc -c '
        eval "$(mise activate bash)"
        cd /path/to/repro
        _mise_hook
        echo "UNSET_ENV=[${UNSET_ENV-<absent>}] SET_ENV=[${SET_ENV-<absent>}]"'
UNSET_ENV=[from_parent] SET_ENV=[dev]
Why this matters in practice: with mise activate in a shell rc, or in CI, or
simply after having run once in a non-dev profile in the same shell, the
variable is already exported before mise evaluates the config — so the false
never takes effect in exactly the situation it is meant for.
Not a duplicate of #12090 / #12389
Both of those concern __MISE_DIFF / prompt-hook session state overriding
values. This is a different mechanism, and the false/unset path is broken
even with that state absent:
$ UNSET_ENV=from_parent MISE_ENV=dev env -u __MISE_DIFF mise exec -- \
      sh -c 'echo [${UNSET_ENV-<absent>}]'
[from_parent]
Also reproduces with __MISE_DIFF never set at all, mise never activated, a
single config file, and no profiles (see the clean-env command above). Plain
string assignment works fine here, whereas in #12389 plain assignment is the case
that works and templates/default are the ones that break — the opposite split.
Root cause analysis
Against main @ c6f6130a03205ee1f9b63142244a8ebff4d1e918.
EnvDirective::Rm records the key in EnvResults.env_remove and drops it from
the in-progress overlay map:
// src/config/env_directive/mod.rs:615-630
EnvDirective::Rm(k, _opts) => {
    ...
    env.shift_remove(&k);
    ...
    r.env_remove.insert(k);
}
Every consumer of env_remove then performs only a map removal:

src/task/mod.rs:2409 — for key in &results.env_remove { env.remove(key); }
src/task/task_context_builder.rs:454 — same
src/config/config_file/mise_toml.rs:1482 — same
src/toolset/toolset_env.rs — final_env() / env_with_path() return
EnvResults but never apply env_remove themselves
src/cli/exec.rs:223 — let mut env = ts.env_with_path(&config).await?; then
cmd.envs(env); env_remove is never consulted
src/cli/env.rs:191 — iterates the set-map calling shell.set_env(k, v);
shell.unset_env is never called

That map is additive: it is layered on top of the inherited environment via
Command::envs, or printed as export lines. Deleting a key from an additive
overlay is a no-op with respect to the parent's value, so env_remove never
becomes a real unset.
The primitives already exist and are used elsewhere in the codebase:

Cmd::env_remove (src/cmd.rs:668) → std::process::Command::env_remove
Shell::unset_env, and EnvDiffOperation::Remove (src/env_diff.rs:34), used
by hook-env / deactivate — #12090 shows hook-env emitting unset MY_VAR,
so the shell-level unset path is reachable, just not wired to env_remove

So the fix looks like plumbing rather than new machinery: apply
env_results.env_remove via Command::env_remove on the exec/run paths, and emit
shell.unset_env(k) for each env_remove key in mise env / hook-env.
Expected behaviour
VAR = false should unset VAR regardless of whether the value came from an
earlier mise config file or from the environment mise was invoked in — matching
the documented "unset a previously set NODE_ENV".
If the current behaviour is intentional and false is only ever meant to cancel
mise-config assignments, the docs should say so explicitly, and there should be a
documented way to unset an inherited variable.

No problems found"},{"number":10065,"title":"Bun only backend","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/10065","updatedAt":"2026-09-02T13:37:08Z","bodyText":"I work in an environment where I'm actively trying to reduce the amount of language ecosystems, and supported tooling, and
one of the things I'm trying to get rid of is node and npm.
There appears to have been some prior work on creating a standalone bun: backend in #2899, which was (sensibly) folded into
the existing npm backend as npm.package_manager = "bun" — matching the pipx/uv pattern. That works great for installing
packages with bun, but it doesn't actually let me drop node/npm from the system: the npm backend still shells out to npm
view for version listing and latest resolution, regardless of which package manager performs the install. The two TODOs at
src/backend/npm.rs:209 and :577 reference exactly this gap.
The blocker called out at the time was that bun view / bun pm view didn't exist (oven-sh/bun#1224). That has since changed -
bun pm view shipped in Bun 1.2.15 (oven-sh/bun#19841), and @risu729 already flagged this on the original PR thread, with
the caveat that switching unconditionally would force every existing npm.package_manager = "bun" user onto a recent bun.
Before I start writing any code, I wanted to check whether you'd be open to a change along these lines, and get your input
on a few scoping questions:

Approach. I'm assuming you'd still prefer this to live inside src/backend/npm.rs rather than as a new bun: backend,
consistent with the #2899 decision. Concretely: when npm.package_manager resolves to bun and the installed bun is new
enough, route _list_remote_versions and latest_stable_version through bun pm view and drop node/npm from get_dependencies /
ensure_npm_for_version_check on that path. Older bun would keep using npm view. Does that shape match what you'd want?
Minimum bun version. bun pm view first shipped in 1.2.15. I'd plan to gate via a version probe analogous to
npm_supports_min_release_age_flag (read from the toolset when bun is mise-managed, fall back to bun --version), and document
the minimum in docs/dev-tools/backends/npm.md. Happy to use a higher minimum if there are known bugs in early versions.
Custom registries. The original PR explicitly kept npm view for custom-registry support. I'll verify whether bun pm view
honors NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY / project-level .npmrc before sending a PR. If it doesn't, the npm-view fallback would need to
stay for users with custom registry configuration — would you want that controlled by an additional setting, or is "use bun
pm view only when no custom registry is configured" sufficient?
Opt-in vs. transparent. Should the node-free path activate automatically whenever bun is the active package manager and
bun pm view is available, or behind an explicit opt-in (e.g. npm.bun_node_free = true) so existing users on older bun don't
see behaviour changes? My preference would be transparent with a version gate, but I'll defer to you here.

Happy to open a draft PR once there's some direction on the above. If this is out of scope or you'd rather it wait, just say
the word and I'll leave it alone."},{"number":12238,"title":"[BUG] Case of `mise run --output keep-order` remove the outputs","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12238","updatedAt":"2026-09-01T23:16:55Z","bodyText":"References

At 2026-08-28T09:56:38Z, minimum_release_age = "24h" caused Codex resolution to skip eligible 0.150.0 and report 0.149.1 as the latest eligible release.
This looks like a mismatch between the shared mise-versions list and the canonical latest-release metadata, rather than a duration-calculation error.
Observed data
GitHub reports:



Release
GitHub published_at




rust-v0.150.0
2026-08-26T19:37:28Z


rust-v0.150.1
2026-08-27T01:56:54Z



At the observation time, 0.150.0 was more than 24 hours old. The upstream Aqua/GitHub version listing contained both 0.150.0 and 0.150.1.
However, the hosted list at https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/codex.toml contained 0.149.1, but no stable 0.150.0 or 0.150.1 entry.
That produces an inconsistent result: the canonical-latest path sees 0.150.1 and correctly excludes it as too new, while the release-age-filtered version-list path cannot see 0.150.0 and falls back to 0.149.1.
Reproduction
$ mise ls-remote codex --minimum-release-age 24h --json
# stable candidate was 0.149.1; 0.150.0 was absent

$ MISE_USE_VERSIONS_HOST=0 MISE_FETCH_REMOTE_VERSIONS_CACHE=0 mise ls-remote codex --minimum-release-age 24h --json
# includes 0.150.0 as the newest eligible stable release
The user-facing symptom from mise update was:
mise WARN newer codex release 0.150.1 ignored by minimum_release_age (24h); latest eligible release is 0.149.1

Possible directions
The smallest fix may be to improve or investigate Codex ingestion/update cadence for mise-versions; it is a cache and temporary lag may be expected.
I also prototyped a client-side safeguard, not a proposed PR yet: when canonical latest metadata says the newest stable release is too new for the cutoff, fetch the backend's upstream version list before choosing the prior eligible release. That avoids choosing an older release solely because the shared list has not caught up, but adds an upstream request in this edge case.
Would maintainers prefer treating the hosted list as authoritative during its normal lag window, or is a direct fallback appropriate specifically for release-age resolution?
AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable; version: unavailable."},{"number":12684,"title":"brew-cask: only the declared artifacts are installed, so codex loses the sibling host it execs","url":"https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12684","updatedAt":"2026-09-01T19:56:27Z","bodyText":"Another brew-cask one. "brew-cask:codex" = "latest" installs cleanly and codex --version reports 0.152.0, but every tool call fails, because the cask ships more than the one binary it declares and only that binary survives the install.
The cask declares a single artifact:
binary "bin/codex"
generate_completions_from_executable "bin/codex", "completion"
while codex-package-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz (sha256 5287a514213f8134210677cce51b23e2eaeaff1925362f18318e4268a5ab1d1b) contains five paths:
bin/codex
bin/codex-code-mode-host
codex-package.json
codex-path/rg
codex-resources/zsh/bin/zsh

Afterwards the Caskroom directory holds the declared binary and the generated completions, and nothing else:
/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/codex/0.152.0/
├── .mise-cask.toml
├── bin/codex
├── etc/bash_completion.d/codex
└── share/…

codex-package.json is the manifest the binary reads to find the rest of its own layout, so losing it costs more than the file itself:
{
  "layoutVersion": 1,
  "version": "0.152.0",
  "entrypoint": "bin/codex",
  "resourcesDir": "codex-resources",
  "pathDir": "codex-path"
}
Codex 0.152.0 runs every tool call through a codex-code-mode-host subprocess. With no host beside the binary it falls back to whatever other copy is on the machine — here the 0.151.0-alpha.7.1 host bundled inside ChatGPT.app — and every command, down to /usr/bin/true, dies before dispatch:
failed to read code-mode host message: failed to decode code-mode IPC frame: missing field `code_mode_host_duration_ns`

The older host never emits that field and the 0.152.0 decoder requires it, so nothing looks wrong until an upgrade moves the CLI ahead of the stale host. Extracting the four missing paths back into the Caskroom directory fixed it here with no other change, which is what points at the install rather than at Codex.
I take the Homebrew behaviour to be staging the whole extracted payload in the Caskroom and symlinking only the declared artifacts out of it, which leaves the siblings where the binary expects them. I can't confirm that side by side — this machine has no Homebrew, which is rather the point of installing casks through mise.
Any cask whose binary resolves resources relative to itself would hit this, so it seemed worth reporting past the one package. Happy to re-run with MISE_VERBOSE=1 and attach output.
